newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Bans to disrupt South Australia grain harvest.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Bans to disrupt South Australia grain harvest.

text.p: Rolling work bans beginning from Wednesday at grain terminals around South Australia are set to disrupt the state's estimated 5.4 million tonne 1996/97 harvest which began this week.

Australian Workers Union State secretary Bob Sneath told Reuters about 400 workers would participate in the rolling bans at South Australian Co-operative Bulk Handling (SACBH) terminals at Wallaroo, Port Pirie, Ardrossan, Port Giles, Port Lincoln and Thevenard.
Under the bans, workers would refuse to load ships or move grain from country terminals to ports, although there would be no restrictions on unloading farmers' trucks into silos.
"At least the farmer can get his (grain) in there, but if the dispute goes on for much longer we will have to look at that as well," Sneath said.
South Australia Farmers' Federation spokesman John Lush said he was relieved farmers would be able to unload their grain, as there had been fears a dispute could result in downgraded quality.
However he said the dispute would still have an impact on the state's reliability as a grain supplier.
"We have got some pretty severe competition in the world at the moment, it is a buyers' market and any disadvantage we have got will blow us completely out of the world market," he said.
Lush said farmers primarily on the state's far west coast had begun harvesting earlier this week, with large numbers expected to start up in the next week.
The state Primary Industries Department has upgraded its estimate for the 1996/97 harvest to 5.4 million tonnes, slightly down on 1995/96's record 5.5 million.
The department estimates the wheat harvest at 2.63 million tonnes, and barley at two million tonnes.
Sneath said union officials hoped to meet again with the SACBH later this week in an effort to resolve the dispute over wage increases and productivity improvements.
